Sociology

Context! Context! Context!

Or, location! Location! Location!

Where?With whom?Under what conditions?

Focuses on the study of diverse social contexts within which society influences individuals.

Seeks to:

  • Understand human lives—behavior, belief, attitude, well-being, and more—by referring to locations in social contexts.
  • Identify and explain patterns.
  • Use sociological imagination and scientific tools.
06 / 18↓

What is a society?

A fellowship, communion, unity, association.

Latin: societās; societātem (accusative); societātis (genitive).

“God is faithful: by whom you are called unto the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.”

1 Corinthians 1:9 · fidelis Deus per quem vocati estis in societātem Filii eius Iesu Christi Domini nostri (Latin Vulgate)
07 / 18↓

Sociology

The study of being together.

“Socio-”: the Latin socius, “companion,” or “fellowship.” “-ology”: from the Greek logos, “study of.”

  • Premise: “No man is an island.” To understand social life fully, we must go beyond the individual.
  • Importance: Comte called sociology the “Queen of Social Sciences.” It covers a broad range of areas, overlapping with anthropology, political science, economics, psychology, and more.
08 / 18↓

The birth of the discipline · mid–late 19th century

New social worlds created new social questions.

Industrialization: growth of factories and large-scale goods production.
Urbanization: growth of cities in the United States, Europe, and elsewhere.
Immense social change: emerging social problems.
Development of science: scientific methods began to be used to study the social world.

10 / 18↓

The birth of the discipline

From an emerging field to a scientific discipline.

1

The first department of sociology was established at the University of Chicago in 1892 by Albion Woodbury Small (1854–1926).

2

Émile Durkheim (1858–1917) founded the first European department of sociology at the University of Bordeaux in 1895.

3

Today, sociology has become a United States-centered scientific discipline, with most sociologists living in the United States.

11 / 18↓

Sociological imagination

A term coined by C. Wright Mills.

The process of identifying a public issue by reflecting on personal experiences of our own—or others’—and viewing individual experiences through the social contexts that shape them.
12 / 18↓

Sociological imagination

“The sociological imagination enables us to grasp the connection between history and biography.”

Biography

An individual’s specific experiences.

History

Socio-historical context: location in the broad stream of events.

Practice your sociological imagination

How does the timing of your birth shape your destiny?

Think about the historical events, economic conditions, social institutions, and cultural expectations that surround a birth cohort.

14 / 18↓

Children of the Great Depression · Glen H. Elder, Jr.

A comparative study of life-course experiences.

Oakland Growth Study

167 children born in Oakland, California, in 1920–1921.

Berkeley Guidance Study

248 children born in Berkeley, California, in 1928–1929.

Both birth cohorts spent part of their childhood in the Great Depression (1929–1939). Which would be more adversely affected? Which would be more resilient?

15 / 18↓

Children of the Great Depression

A comparative study of life-course experiences.

16 / 18↓

Children of the Great Depression · Pattern found

The same historical event did not have the same effects on every cohort.

Oakland cohort

A great many children in the Oakland sample succeeded in rising above childhood disadvantages and in achieving a full life into the seventh decade.

Berkeley cohort

Berkeley children were more adversely influenced by the economic collapse than were Oakland adolescents.
